summary: This note is a long encyclopedia-style overview of the ocean, covering its extent and division into five principal oceans, its vertical and horizontal zones, and its temperature, salinity and sea ice. It also describes ocean currents, the origin of Earth's oceans, coastal and wave processes, tides, and the ocean's depth and volume. The clipped text breaks off mid-sentence while discussing how oceans moderate climate.
one_line: Overview of the world ocean covering its extent, zones, temperature, currents, origin, waves, tides, depth and coastal processes.
key_facts: The ocean covers about 70.8% of Earth's surface and contains 97% of Earth's water.
The ocean is customarily divided into five principal oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Antarctic/Southern and Arctic.
The photic zone is defined as the depth at which light intensity is only 1% of the surface value, approximately 200 m in the open ocean.
Photosynthesis in the photic zone produces half of the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere.
In the tropics, surface ocean temperatures can rise to over 30 °C (86 °F), while near the poles the temperature in equilibrium with sea ice is about −2 °C (28 °F).
Deep ocean temperatures range between −2 °C (28 °F) and 5 °C (41 °F) in all parts of the globe.
The major ocean currents named in the note are the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio Current, Agulhas Current and Antarctic Circumpolar Current.
The average depth of the oceans is 3,688 meters (12,100 ft).
The maximum depth of the Mariana Trench has been estimated at 10,971 meters (35,994 ft); the Trieste reached the bottom in 1960 with a crew of two men.
The longest continuous mountain range is the global mid-oceanic ridge system, at 65,000 km (40,000 mi), several times longer than the Andes.
Oceanographers state that less than 20% of the oceans have been mapped.
Pillow basalt from the Isua Greenstone Belt provides evidence that water existed on Earth 3.8 billion years ago.
Oceanic tidal ranges in the Bay of Fundy and Ungava Bay in Canada reach up to 16 meters.
The ocean is known to be the habitat of over 230,000 species but may hold perhaps over two million species.
Point Nemo, the ocean's furthest pole of inaccessibility, is roughly 2,688 km (1,670 mi) from the nearest land.
